Is the truth closer to “I live the life I want with diabetes” vs “I’m not defined by diabetes” or “I am more than diabetes?”
.
I’ve been thinking about the conditional joy mindset of “I can have fun if my sugars are in range” or “I can be happy if my sugars are in range” and I’m working on living more alongside my numbers vs in them. 
.
After all, is it so wrong to be defined by diabetes in some ways?

I drove down to @campbluebonnet this week to speak to the kids about my life with T1D. Camps are so important. They need our support and participation. Camps of all sizes survive on the support of participants, individual donors, corporate sponsors and grants. They’re run almost exclusively by volunteers and without the passion of the alumni and staff, would not be able to have the profound impact on their campers every year. 
.
Something I can talk about forever is the importance of getting outside, making friends and trying new things outside of your comfort zone. Camps are critical to the development of our children, and camps designed for children with disabilities are especially important. 
.
So I encourage all of you in this diabetes sphere or online community or wherever to log off and give your heart, time and money to a diabetes camp. It could make the difference that changes someone’s life. Thank you @drhannahparr for inviting me to be part of this special camp in the heart of Texas 🤠

Literally minutes before this comment came in, my diabetes phone died while I was out of the house. I had no way to check my glucose or dose insulin - luckily my pump was running in the background, but I laughed when I saw this comment because this app can cause us all to compare ourselves to others so quickly, and things are not always what they seem. There’s a lot of talk about “getting out of your comfort zone”, but what does that look like in practice? 
.
One of my basketball coaches told me that I needed to “search for butt whoopings” so I could keep improving. For diabetes this could look like exploring things outside your routine like exercise, food or device placement. For basketball it could be going to a new gym where you don’t know anyone. In business it could be going to a new networking group or challenging yourself to learn something new or try out a different process. 
.
You learn more about who you are when you put yourself somewhere unfamiliar.

There’s so much to be grateful for in spite of the grief, heaviness, challenges, expenses and inconveniences. Thank you to @campbluebonnet for the photos that remind me how much there is to be grateful for.

Six months into 2026, here’s what the search for living well with T1D has actually taught me. 

Some, I expected. A few caught me off guard (see my thoughts on a cure on slide 3). 

The biggest takeaway was a reminder that it’s all about mastering the basics with intention and structure. 

Comment “podcast” and I’ll send you my top 3 @diabeticsdoingthings episodes from this year for you to watch and dig in.

21 years with T1D and here’s what I wish people understood: the hardest part of a low isn’t always the shaking or dizziness or fear of seeing those double arrows down.

It’s losing your words mid-sentence in a meeting and hoping no one noticed. Once I just kept repeating “mannnn” at the end of every sentence.

It’s snapping at someone you love and not realizing why.

It’s the wave of doom that hits out of nowhere. This one is so real for me. Anxiety with no logic, just biology.

It’s not being able to shake the brain fog hours after being back in range. 

It’s waking up in the middle of the night soaked in sweat and showing up to work like nothing happened.

It’s being told you seem “off” or “moody” when your brain is running out of fuel.

We’re not distracted or rude and sometimes we’re not fine. We’re managing something invisible, in real time, while doing everything else you CAN see.

If you love someone with T1D, share this. Sometimes the low no one sees is the one that needs the most grace.

What do you wish people could see? 👇

21+ years with T1D and here’s the thing about high blood sugar: they affect me way worse than lows, but lows always get the urgency while highs get the silence.

The crankiness. 
The unquenchable thirst. 
Wanting to go for a walk but being stuck on a plane or in a conference room. 
Desperate to get your sugars in range to just feel normal again. Feeling that sigh of relief when you break a sweat as the insulin hits. 

Going back to the same email three times because your brain is processing slowly. Getting distracted because you can’t stop thinking about getting your sugars down. 

The urge to cancel plans because you feel like you were in a car wreck. Being called flaky instead of sick.

It’s the guilt spiral. Because somehow a high always feels like your fault, even when you did everything right.

You dose, you wait, you could feel like garbage for HOURS and you’re expected to function the entire time while you have your finger on the trigger of a rage bolus. 

Nobody rushes to help you with a high. There’s no “quick, eat this.” Just a correction, and patience you don’t have. I like when people are vulnerable online and share the highs, it feels nice to have someone who understands. 

The highs deserve grace just as much as the lows. 💙

What do you wish people understood about highs? 👇

Choosing a new insulin pump? Here is how I would approach such a decision.
.
We live in such a vast richness of shared lived experience thanks to the internet. Unfortunately, that doesn’t necessarily mean ideal options will be available for each of us, and choosing a medical device is a deeply personal decision so there’s a lot to consider. 
.
I’m currently using an insulin pump as part of a clinical trial, so it’s caused me to think about all the different factors that go into a big decision like a medical device. 📟📈📉
.
What’d I miss?

The will to win is only exceeded by the preparation to win. You can’t cheat the game, you gotta put in reps! Skill acquisition takes intentional repetition and time under tension. 
.
Everybody wants to be under the lights on game day. Not everybody wants to balance a broom on their hand after working a full day AND going to the cardiologist. This is why we’ll win.

One of my close friends asked me “What are you bullish about in Marketing/Advertising in 2026?” and I hadn’t been asked that in a while. 

But right away I started thinking of the big themes from the first half of this year, and a few things really stood out. So just past the halfway point of 2026, here’s what I’m bullish on in marketing 👇

1️⃣ Distribution is moat. Creator-led businesses have a massive edge. Storytelling + production + distribution + an audience that already trusts you = unfair advantage. @askcatgpt and @jun_yuh had an incredible discussion about this on a recent podcast. 

2️⃣ The solopreneur. AI has erased the skill gaps that used to stop people from starting. No code? No website? No funding? AI solves this already.

3️⃣ Niche, wins. The more specific you are, the easier it is for the algorithm — and your people — to find you.

What are you bullish on? Let me know 👇

Sorry for choosing violence on the TL, but I’ve been thinking a lot about the popularized and resonant words that “people with T1D make 180 additional decisions per day.” Frankly, that’s too many decisions. 
.
My approach to decision making is one I’ve adapted from Jim Collins and Peter Drucker where I look for single decisions that remove hundreds or thousands of other decisions downstream. To paraphrase Collins, “Don’t make 100 decisions when one will do.” Then you can begin to realize that a whole lot of decisions that look like different decisions are really part of the same category of a decision.
.
This is often popularized in “decision fatigue” articles written about Steve Jobs and his trademarked Issey Miyake turtlenecks and Levi’s. As people with diabetes who are far more prone to chronic fatigue, it’s helpful to remove or batch decisions where possible. For me, that looks like automated insulin delivery and planning my meals as much as I can.

You want to be successful? Congrats, so does everyone. Here’s some of what it takes to be good, not great, at anything. To achieve greatness you must first be willing to suck. If you can do this, you can do anything.
These were my 2026 New Year’s resolutions and I’ll never go back on them. Become religious about them and see your life change. They are simple but not easy.
You want to be insulin sensitive? Lock in on the basics. Sleep, water, strength training and breathing. All the insulin in the world won’t lower your glucose if your body can’t do anything with it.

Health and optimization culture is obsessed with longevity, but I think we’re missing the target. Resilience is a much more worthwhile target.
